sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know *aun cuando* "even when, even if" from B2 Unit 8. It follows the same rule as *aunque*: the indicative for a fact, the subjunctive for a possibility. It is more formal and more emphatic, which suits the language of treaties, bridges and borders.

sections.title: Fact or possibility?
rows: Aun cuando Guyana y Surinam están cerca de Brasil, durante mucho tiempo no tuvieron carreteras hacia él.
Aun cuando se construyan más puentes, la selva seguirá siendo difícil de cruzar.
a possibility: subjunctive (more bridges may be built)
Aun cuando tienen idiomas distintos, los países de CARICOM trabajan juntos.
a fact: indicative (they have different languages)
Aunque tienen idiomas distintos, los países de CARICOM trabajan juntos.

items.spanish: Aun cuando Brasil y Guyana son vecinos, hasta 2009 no hubo un puente sobre el río Takutu.
items.english: Even though Brazil and Guyana are neighbours, until 2009 there was no bridge over the Takutu river.

items.spanish: Aun cuando se construyan más puentes, la selva seguirá siendo difícil de cruzar.
items.english: Even if more bridges are built, the jungle will remain hard to cross.

items.spanish: Aun cuando tienen idiomas distintos, los países de CARICOM trabajan juntos.
items.english: Even though they have different languages, the CARICOM countries work together.

items.spanish: Los dos países seguirán hablando aun cuando no estén de acuerdo.
items.english: The two countries will keep talking even if they do not agree.

sections.content: Ask whether the speaker presents the obstacle as a real fact (indicative) or as something possible that will not change the plan (subjunctive). Write *aun* without an accent in *aun cuando*; with an accent, *aún* means "still".
